utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. To keep matters short, for the record, I see appearances for the Prosecution are Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, accompanied by Mr. Saxon, and by Ms. Katalinic. I also see another new face. Could you please introduce the new member of the team?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You see here with us Ms. Melissa Pack. You know her already from submissions. She is now a trial attorney in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Mr. Seselj, I see that you are present, you are representing yourself and I also see present as standby counsel, Mr. Hooper, assisted by co-stand-by counsel, Mr. O'Shea, and accompanied by ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Accompanied by our case manager, Lea Kulinowski and Ms. Nassira Hayaty who sits behind, who is from The Hague, and who has joined us as an intern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for introducing these team members, Mr. Hooper. I would like to start this Status Conference with inviting the registrar to report to the Chamber whether any progress has been made in terms of practical facilities to be provided to you, Mr. Seselj, when you asked at the last Status Conference, be provided with the same facilities as the late Mr. Milosevic had at the time. So therefore, could I invite you, Mister representative of the Registry, to inform the Chamber and the parties about any progress made.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Upon the request of the Presiding Judge and following the Status Conference of the 3rd of November, 2006, during which Mr. Seselj made several oral requests for facilities to be provided to him to facilitate the preparation of his defence, the Registry would like to inform both the Chamber and the accused as follows. To date, the Registry has provided the following facilities to Mr. Seselj at the United Nations Detention Unit. Number one, a cell in addition to his residential cell, where Mr. Seselj is able to store case-related material; number 2, a video player in Mr. Seselj's residential cell; 3, a back-up video player; and four, an audio tape player in Mr. Seselj's residential cell. In addition, the Registry has offered or otherwise made available to Mr. Seselj the following facilities, of which, to date, he has refused to avail himself. Number one, the services of a technical or administrative assistant from the Registry to provide support to the accused. Number two, a desktop computer in Mr. Seselj's cell at the UNDU. Three, the assistance of stand-by counsel as per the deputy registrar's decision of 30th October 2006. The registrar is currently considering the oral requests made by Mr. Seselj at the Status Conference of the 3rd of November, 2006, and which include the following facilities: 1, a second cell with adjoining access to his residential cell, which Mr. Seselj would use as an office and whose key Mr. Seselj wants to keep in his pocket. 2, a privileged telephone and fax within the said office. 3, the appointment by the Registry of Mr. Seselj's legal associates. In this regard, the registrar notes that the accused has previously requested this facility but has failed to comply with the conditions for the recognition of his legal associates by the registrar. The matter has been litigated before the president who affirmed the registrar's approach. 4, privileged access to Mr. Seselj's legal associates by using the above-mentioned facilities. 5, privileged access to his investigators and potential witnesses by using the above-mentioned facilities. The registrar is currently considering the accused's oral requests made at the 3rd November, 2006 Status Conference. A written decision is expected to be issued next week. In his decision, the registrar will inform Mr. Seselj of which of the requested facilities, if any, can be provided to him. In addition, the registrar will inform Mr. Seselj of the legal criteria applied in assessing his requests. These criteria will be applied when considering any future requests for facilities made by the accused. A copy of the registrar's decision will be provided to the Trial Chamber for information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Seselj, this updates you on what the Registry is preparing at this moment, and as you may have heard, a decision on all of your requests is expected to be issued next week.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something to say too in relation to that, Mr. Orie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may do so, Mr. Seselj. Could you inform us about what kind of things would you like to further explain your requests so that it can be taken into consideration or is there -- because if the decision will be issued in the beginning of next week, of course it would be important to know what that decision is before commenting on it. But if it would contribute to the quality of the decision, then you have an opportunity to speak at this moment, Mr. Seselj. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the representative of the Registry has for the umpteenth time insisted on his opinion that my legal advisors do not meet the criteria of the Registry. The Registry is trying to impose defence counsel criteria on my associates and such criteria should not be applied to my associates. I will never be able to meet those criteria then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this sounds very repetitious to me. This matter has been raised various times, and I think your position is perfectly clear. If, in addition to decisions taken by the Trial Chamber or by the Appeals Chamber, anything new should be introduced, then you are invited to do so. But you are not invited to repeat positions that have been expressed at various other occasions. Is there anything else you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then, Mr. Orie, you should caution the Registry as well. They cannot go on repeating the same positions time and again. For as long as they keep repeating their positions, I react to them, because I simply cannot agree to that. There is no legal basis for what they've been doing. In actual fact, they are trying to prevent me from preparing my defence. That's the only reason. An audio player was first referred to here and now. I don't need an audio player. I never got one. If they offer me one, I'm not going to take it because I don't need it. A video player I do need, for the video cassettes from the court proceedings. So this is something that I had already agreed upon at the time of pre-trial. Judge Schomburg, when I asked for recordings of Status Conferences in the Serbian language, I was offered video recordings. Then once the trial starts, that I receive video recordings again. I saw that but now the Registry is trying to impose something else on me, an audio player. It is very important, Mr. Orie. Oh, you're so impatient. You don't have time to listen to me, to hear me out and that's very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I would just like to say that the only thing the representative of the Registry did is to tell the Chamber what had been provided to you in the United Nations Detention Unit. As far as an audio tape player is concerned, if the Chamber would decide that what you might expect soon, certain material to be disclosed to you in audio format, then you would need an audio player to listen to that material. That's one -- I'm interested to know since you complained last time about the video player not functioning, I now see at least the representative of the registrar informed us that a video player was provided to you in your residential cell and a back-up video player as well. Are the complaints about the functioning of these video players, are they dealt with?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about this reserve video player. I got this other video player for the time being. I haven't got any problems with it. But I insist, yet again, that I state my views on the audio player. I think that is very important. And you're not letting me do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps at the end of the hearing, if that is -- if I give you an opportunity to raise any additional matters. Until now, we only heard that an audio tape player has been provided to you. At a later stage, if there's any relevant issue to be raised in that respect, you will get an opportunity to do so. Anything else you'd like to add to it, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, you didn't put it right, that I got an audio player. I got a video player, Mr. Orie. Now you presented an inaccurate fact. I only got a video player and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I didn't say that you got an audio player. I only said that the representative of the Registry informed us, so that's his report, that you got an audio player. You will have an opportunity at the end of this hearing to further comment on whether you received it and what further comments you have. I'd like then to move, unless there's anything else that, Mr. Seselj, you'd like to raise at this moment, in relation to the report, the progress report by the Registry. If not, then I'll move to the second issue, that is, the reduction of the indictment. The parties are hereby informed that prior to the start of this Status Conference, I signed a decision by this Chamber reducing the scope of the indictment. I take it that it has been filed, meanwhile, and I will just set out, since it's -- you have not received it yet. No translation is yet available, just to inform you, to update. I will inform you about the content of that decision. The decision -- the Chamber has issued its decision on the application of Rule 73 bis. The Chamber will now inform you briefly of the content of its decision. On the 31st of August of this year, the Chamber invited the Prosecution to make proposals for the reduction of the indictment. This invitation was initially declined, but led, ultimately, to the filing of the Prosecution's submission on proposals to reduce the scope of the indictment. In that submission, the Prosecution made a number of suggestions, namely, the dropping of cumulative counts and the dropping of charges relating to Western Slavonia, Brcko, Bijeljina, and one crime site in the Nevesinje municipality set out in paragraph 27 of the indictment. At the previous Status Conference, the accused was asked whether he would like to make submissions on the matter, which he declined, requesting only that he receives a full modified version of the indictment when the process has been completed. In its decision, the Trial Chamber accepts all of the proposals made by the Prosecution in its submission on proposals to reduce the scope of the indictment. Therefore, evidence will not be presented in respect of the charges relating to the crime sites of western Slavonia, Brcko, Bijeljina, and the crime site of Boracko Jezero or Mount Borasnica as currently described in paragraph 27 of the indictment. In addition, the Trial Chamber finds that evidence will not be presented in respect of the charges relating to the crime site of Bosanski Samac. However, the Prosecution may present what the Trial Chamber has termed, and I quote, "non-crime-base evidence" in respect of the crime sites of Western Slavonia, Brcko, Bijeljina, Bosanski Samac, and the crime site of Boracko Jezero/Mount Borasnica. The decision sets out what types of evidence are considered non-crime-base evidence. Examples include, pattern evidence and evidence that goes to proof of the purpose and methods of the joint criminal enterprise charged in the indictment. The Prosecution shall indicate the changes made to the indictment in accordance with the Chamber's decision, by the substitution of the relevant parts of the indictment with the words in square brackets and I quote "Omitted pursuant to Rule 73 bis D of the Rules and the decision of the Trial Chamber dated the 8th of November 2006." This completes the summary of our decision. In relation to the indictment, and I am now addressing the Prosecution, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, in relation to the indictment, the Chamber has one question on -- what we consider to be a minor matter and that's not raised in the Chamber's decision. The Prosecution is invited to clarify and either now or at another occasion if you should require further time to prepare, the significance, if it has any, of the phrase, I quote, "the Dubrovnik Republic" which is found in paragraph 6 of the indictment. But the reference to the Dubrovnik Republic is not found in any other part of the indictment, so the Chamber wonders whether it is of any consequence to your case. As I said before, it is -- we consider this at this moment to be a minor point. Do you want to respond to it right away or would you rather delay your response.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can actually right away explain this express used and why it is only used in paragraph 6. In paragraph 6 of the indictment, we address the purpose and the scope of the joint criminal enterprise. We, in particular, list the territories that were targeted by the joint criminal enterprise and that is the reason why the term "Dubrovnik republic" is used in the indictment because the region around Dubrovnik and Dubrovnik itself was targeted to become part of Greater Serbia. The Prosecution will not lead any evidence related to events in Dubrovnik because that's not the scope of this indictment. We will only provide documents such as the programme of the Serbian Radical Party or the programme of the Serbian Chetnik movement which actually refers to Dubrovnik as to become part of Greater Serbia. In addition, we will actually present the expert witness Tomic, a historian, who will address the so-called Dubrovnik republic as being part of the historical concept of Greater Serbia, pursued long before the accused and that the accused then actually referred to himself again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, you're now explaining what kind of evidence you will lead on the matter. My question was not what evidence we could expect but, mainly, on what the Dubrovnik republic, what its role was in the indictment. I do understand that, although it is the Prosecution's case that the Dubrovnik republic was not outside the scope of the joint criminal enterprise, that nevertheless, none of the crimes charged to Mr. Seselj committed through the joint criminal enterprise is situated in the Dubrovnik Republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And we mention it basically for completeness purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have no further matters in relation to the indictment to be raised. Is there anything you, Mr. Seselj, or you, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, would like to raise in relation to the indictment, that is, what we find in the indictment, what now the scope of the indictment is?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have a question. Have you set a deadline, a time limit for the Prosecution by which they are supposed to give me the amended indictment? It's very important for me to have the proper text, the redacted text, so that at every point in time, I know exactly what the indictment contains and what it doesn't contain. That has to be very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Seselj, you are talking about an amended indictment, whether we should call it an amended indictment. Under Rule 73 bis is another matter, because under Rule 73 bis(F), there is a possibility, although we are not envisioning at this moment that it will be used, but you never know, that parts of the indictment on which no evidence is led could later be varied again. To be very practical, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, could you tell us when -- how much time would you need, you think, to produce an indictment with the relevant portions replaced by omitted pursuant to Rule, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that can easily be done in two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can easily be done in two days. Then take it that since not much text will change, that it's mainly taking out and substituting the portions taken out by one line always the same, that even before you are finished that, perhaps you could already apply for that line to be translated so it can immediately be put in place in the B/C/S version of the indictment as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Seselj, on the basis of the answer given by Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, I take it that it will take not more than two or three days for you to receive such -- the new indictment in its redacted format. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Orie, perhaps there was a problem with the interpretation. I did not say amended indictment, I said reduced indictment. Amended is in the broader sense, but reduced is reduced. Basically, it was not amended, it was reduced. Maybe there was a problem with the interpretation. I was very precise but the interpreter was not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That was exactly what the speaker said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the interpreters confirm that at least that's how I understood it, that he used the word reduced indictment. There is no reason at this moment to further explore that matter. If you find it of great importance, I couldn't see at this moment that it would be of great importance, apart from the general point, of course, translation should be as precise as possible, then of course you always could have reviewed the original tapes, see what you said, see what the interpreters said. At this moment, there is no need to further explore that. You have explained now what you meant to say and that's understood by the Chamber. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, I think that at this point in time, that's not really important, but it may happen during the trial, that some things are really important and there may be a misinterpretation. Since the Prosecution can submit within the course of two days the text of the reduced indictment to me, I request that they also give a text of the pre-trial brief. There are two reasons for that. The pre-trial brief was already made in two parts. The first part was made for the first indictment and the second part for the expanded indictment, only for the parts for which the indictment was expanded. Now, since the indictment has been reduced, I believe that all conditions have been met for the Prosecution to stand duty-bound to definitely redact the pre-trial brief. That their pre-trial brief should be in a single body of text, so that on the basis of their pre-trial brief, within the time limit that you set, I submit my own pre-trial defence brief. I cannot do that before I have the single text of the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, which strictly pertains to what is contained in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, since you already made such a request at the last Status Conference, the Chamber has given this request already some thought and therefore, the Trial Chamber immediately decides on your repeated request. At the last Status Conference, you observed that if the indictment is reduced, that the Prosecution should be ordered to amend its pre-trial brief to take account of the changes made to the indictment. The Chamber does not agree with you, as explained before, the indictment will be reduced only to the extent of removing certain counts and factual allegations. The indictment is the central instrument giving notice to an accused about the allegations brought against them and that pre-trial brief does not have a comparably important role. It should be clear to you from the newly-amended indictment which parts of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief have been rendered obsolete, therefore, your request that the Prosecution be required to make changes to its pre-trial brief is denied. Mr. Seselj, we are talking about pre-trial briefs at this moment and you have raised the issue of time limit to be set for you producing a pre-trial brief. Before I continue with the pre-trial brief, you are, being your own counsel, Mr. Seselj, you are entitled at the beginning of the trial, to make an opening statement in accordance with Rule 84 and moreover, as an accused, you may be allowed, at the Chamber's discretion, to make an unsworn statement under the control of the Chamber. That would be in accordance with Rule 84 bis. Could you, to start with, inform the Chamber whether you wish to make, first of all, an opening statement, and second, to make an unsworn statement under Rule 84 bis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have planned to make an opening statement during the second part of the trial, after the OTP has presented his case and called all his witnesses, and at the beginning of the presentation of the Defence case. But immediately following the opening statement of the Prosecutor, I should like to make an accused's statement, if you inform me how much time I shall have at my disposal, and if I am allocated approximately the same time as that allotted to Mr. Milosevic for his statement as an accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you inform us how much time was allocated to Mr. Milosevic and whether that was an unsworn statement under Rule 84 bis or whether that was an opening statement? Of course we could check in the public records, but since you seem to be aware of it, if you could inform us, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The opening statement of the Defence by Mr. Milosevic was made during the first part -- second part of the trial, and his accused statement followed the opening statement of the Prosecutor, and I have the transcripts of the trial of Mr. Milosevic which were published in the magazine, the Serbian Free Thought. In my estimation, I would require at least three hours for the statement of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider your request to be granted three hours to make a statement under Rule 84 bis, and I do understand that you have now announced that you have elected to make an opening statement at the beginning of the Defence case, if it ever comes to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean if it ever comes to that? I sure hope I will not die too, Mr. Orie. I sure hope that I will be able to endure this process throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this was an inappropriate remark, but what I meant, and of course you could ask me, what I meant is to say that if, after the presentation of the Prosecution's case, there would be a judgement of acquittal, that there would be no need to make an opening statement at the beginning of the Defence case which will then not follow. That's what I had in mind, just for your information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Mr. Orie, but the first thing which occurred to me is that perhaps I might die during the trial. I'm sorry. I withdraw my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's accepted. This about opening statements and unsworn statements, the other matter I'd like to raise is a submission that was filed by the Prosecution yesterday in English. So therefore, you will not have seen that submission yet, because it has not yet been translated. It relates to a matter you raised during the last Status Conference, to the various submissions you made to the Prosecution on what you called "special defences" under Rule 67(A)(i). I told you that we would return to that. And what I first would like to do is invite the Prosecution to just summarily present the content of your yesterday's notification so that Mr. Seselj is at least aware of what it contains.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before I begin, Your Honour, we have brought additional copies of this submission, if you would like them to be distributed. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Do you mean in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If it would enlighten the parties present, we have several copies of a document that summarises the submissions of the accused. This is in -- which summarise the submissions and disclosures of the accused under Rule 67. If this would further assist the parties and the Chamber, I would be perfectly happy to turn these over right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, since Mr. Seselj can't read it at this moment, you're invited to orally present in a summary which you would like to bring to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Very briefly, the Prosecution submission filed yesterday summarised the disclosures pursuant to Rule 67 made by this accused since 2003, two of which were actually filed with the Registry. Those were submissions 103 and 104. Very briefly, Your Honour. The Prosecution believes that none of these disclosures or submissions fall within the scope of Rule 67(A), rather, they address issues raised in the indictment and in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. They address substantive issues nor do they address or name any potential witnesses that this accused might call in support of any so-called special defence. They are more analogous, Your Honour, to a defence pre-trial brief than any kind of notice pertaining to a special defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give examples of -- just to focus any argument on the matter, could you give us some examples where you say "This is raised but this is a matter which is in our view not a special defence" as we find it under Rule 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For example, Your Honour, submissions 103 and 104, frankly, are attacks made against two potential Prosecution witnesses, attacking their reliability and credibility. Submission number 136, Your Honour, is a submission related to the issue of hate speech and whether this accused could be convicted or not for using hate speech during the war in the former Yugoslavia. In the Prosecution's submission, Your Honour, these matters do not fall within the scope of Rule 67. Submission 147 and 162 deal with the crimes allegedly committed by John Paul I, the Roman Catholic Pope, as well as the genocidal politics of the Vatican towards the Serbian people. And it goes on and on and on, Your Honour. Some of them for hundreds, one of them for over 2.000 pages. So in the Prosecution's submissions, Your Honour, these materials do not properly fall within the scope of Rule 67(A).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you seek any particular relief, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, we do not, Your Honour. We provided this submission as a form of bringing more clarity to this issue for all the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Seselj, where you said you had notified the Prosecution of special defences, there seems to be some disagreement on whether these notifications contain any special defences. I asked Mr. Saxon specifically to give a few examples in order to make it possible, perhaps, to focus, on the basis of these examples, to see what the disagreement actually is. And I heard him saying that one of the notifications explained that hate speech -- let me just look at what exactly he said. "Hate speech and whether the accused could be convicted or not for using hate speech during the war in the former Yugoslavia." Now, I understand that hate speech is in the indictment presented as one of the means of the contributions of the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Seselj, from what I now understand, you seem to challenge or want to challenge that a hate speech could be a way of contributing to a joint criminal enterprise, which could result in criminal responsibility for crimes committed through such a joint criminal enterprise. The second example Mr. Saxon mentioned is that, in one of these notifications, you have pointed at crimes allegedly committed by the Roman Catholic Pope. Could you explain to us, perhaps, first of all, why you consider this special defences under Rule 67?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, Mr. Saxon has not informed properly you and your colleagues. Through these concepts of mine of a special defence, and this is a single special defence concept, as part of which I have submitted a number of notifications to the OTP, I'm not primarily contesting hate speech as a form of a criminal offence. I will be challenging it during the trial and in my pre-trial brief, but what I'm doing is exhaustively informing the OTP in the form of a specific concept of defence of the hate speech of Croatian officials, of Muslim officials in Bosnia, of foreign, western statesmen, Jacques Chirac, Bill Clinton and many others. And of course I'm not invoking any witnesses in that, but I am invoking documents, namely, papers, books, et cetera. And all this is marked and all the sources are properly indicated. So that Mr. Saxon has actually misinterpreted the content of my specific special defence concept. Furthermore, within this concept, I challenge the very concepts of a JCE, that is true, but within my concept of special defence, on the basis of exerts from my public speeches, I show that not only did I not spread hate speech and therefore spread propaganda in favour of the commission of criminal offences, but rather on the contrary, opposed the commission of criminal offences and pointed to the need to abide by the provisions of international laws of war by all soldiers and by all our troops, wherever the combat operations were. As part of this concept, I informed the OTP that some potential witnesses had been police confidantes of the communist police in Yugoslavia at a certain point of time in the past. And it was on the basis of police records about their activity, namely, some of them were spies of western intelligence services, I submitted that information to the OTP in advance as a special form of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you are explaining to us what you are setting out in these notifications. It all sounds, in my ears, very much as just your defence. Therefore, I specifically asked you why you consider what seems to be important matters for your defence, why they would fall within the scope of the special defences under Rule 67(A)(i)(b). As an example -- would you, please, not interrupt me, Mr. Seselj. One special defence is mentioned there, diminished or lack of mental responsibility. Just as with the other example given in 67(A) under (i)(a) where it's called alibi, these are very special kind of defences which should be known to the Prosecution in order to properly present its case. What you just told us is legal argument, is challenging that the Prosecution could ever prove that it's an evidentiary matter, but I have heard nothing until now which would fall within the scope of special defences.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, I have thoroughly studied Rule 67, in particular, item(1)(b). Here, there is a generic determinant which then goes in specifying -- saying including a defence of diminished mental responsibility. Not every special defence is defence invoking diminished mental responsibility. It can be just one of the forms of special defence. I do not intend to plead -- to defend myself by diminished mental responsibility. That is quite clear to you, I hope. But I do have special defence. Why is it special? And that is a crucial question. Because you have not had such a special defence in any other trial before this Court. It is ipso facto special because of that. No one has had such a defence as yet. And, fortunately, I have been here for four years, so I had occasion to really diligently and thoroughly prepare myself. I worked over these past four years and my associates, the entire team worked over these past four years, whereas the OTP, until the last Status Conference, failed to even examine the material which I submitted to them which you could have seen from their reactions a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So just to -- first of all, to avoid whatever misunderstanding, Mr. Seselj, I think everyone agrees that special defences under Rule 67(A)(i)(b) are not limited to the two that are explicitly mentioned there. But listening to you, you said that the defences were special because they were the first to be presented in any case before this Tribunal. May I then specifically ask you that, for example, factual questions or legal argument on the role of a hate speech in the commission of crimes, do you consider them by -- merely by presenting them for the first time before this Tribunal special defences under Rule 67(A)?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I will certainly contest here hate speech as a form of the commission of a crime, because that form of the commission of a criminal offence is something which does not figure in international humanitarian law until the moment of the outbreak of war in the former Yugoslavia -- in the former Yugoslavia. The form which exists is incitement which can be incitement of the direct perpetrator or the direct and public instigation of people to commit -- unidentified people to commit crimes. This is what the OTP could not find and for failure to have such argumentation, it is actually invoking something which international law did not actually have until the outbreak of war in the former Yugoslavia. This is something that I will constantly challenge during the trial. Now, what is a special form of defence? It is my intention to show, through this, through it, that in Croatia, among the Muslims in Bosnia, among the western politicians, leaders and public figures, there were much more intensive, much more vitriolic forms of hate speech than those ascribed to me. I'm trying to pipe down, but of course I cannot always be successful in that. So I'm seeking to prove, through a special form of defence, that the OTP has inappropriately pointed, singled out just me from this whole group of people and events that I have just described a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you intend to prove and call that a special defence that other leaders and western politicians and public figures, that they used forms of hate speech that are far beyond what you have been charged with. Is that a proper understanding of this special defence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this is just one segment of my special form of defence because I bear in mind the practice of this Tribunal of yours, according to which an accused -- if you will just allow me to explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Seselj. You earlier said that you intended to bring the volume of your voice down but you would not always succeed. I nevertheless urge you to try a bit harder and I accept that you might not always succeed, but to just continue on the same level of volume and saying that you will not always succeed doesn't help us out of the problem that at a certain moment, we cannot hear the interpretation anymore. Please proceed and try to do your best in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have tried to the best of my ability, and have studied the former jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the legal practice of it. And I have seen that in all other cases, an accused cannot defend himself by saying others to have committed that crime, others have killed, murdered, others have raped, others have looted, others have destroyed, et cetera. That is your jurisprudence. However, the specificity of my form of defence is based on the fact that the OTP is trying to single out my words from a concrete historical context showing, thereby, me to be some sort of an exception, in actual fact, by making the wrong choice, by pointing to someone who, in this verbal equalibristics, cannot be actually called most radical or the most extreme. So we have to observe this case within its historical context. Through this special form of defence, I wish to emphasise this historical context. If the French president, Jacques Chirac, can insult the Serbian people by using the worst of insults and has no headache over it, it is out of place for me to be put on trial here to be judged here for much milder statements. That is the gist of my special defence concept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will further deal with the special defences issue after the break, after it has had an opportunity to discuss among themselves the submissions you made, both Mr. Saxon and you, Mr. Seselj. Mr. Seselj, at the last Status Conference, you observed that the Chamber had not set a deadline for the submission of the defence pre-trial brief in accordance with Rule 65 ter(F). As you correctly observed, Rule 65 ter(F) provides that the pre-trial Judge shall order the defence to file a pre-trial brief addressing the factual and legal issues in the case, the nature of the defence case, and other matters listed under the Rule. The Rule also states that the defence pre-trial brief should be filed no later than three weeks before the pre-trial conference. For various reasons, including the assignment of counsel between late August and late October 2006, the pre-trial Judge did not set a deadline for the defence pre-trial brief. Mr. Seselj, would you please clarify, first of all, whether you wish to submit a pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, I assume that it's clear to you on the basis of my entire conduct over these past four years, I would not evade that at the cost of life itself. It never crossed my mind to give up on that particular right and that obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then inform you, Mr. Seselj, that generally, a -- the filing of a defence pre-trial brief is looked at, as a rule, which invites the defence to already give a look into what it wants to present and it is usually not looked at as something which is much in favour of the defence. But, of course, if you take a different approach, if you take the approach that it would be in your favour to already inform the Prosecution and the Chamber about what your case will be, similarly, for the same reason, you're not under an obligation to make an opening statement, you want to defer that to a later stage and keep your cards close until that moment, you have an opportunity to do so, and even you already told us that you would use that opportunity. But of course it's up to you. But it's just one observation where you said that you would not give up that right, whereas some people would see it as an obligation they wished not to be under rather than a right one could exercise. But I leave it to you, Mr. Seselj. Do I understand that you wish to file a pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, I feel so superior in relation to the Prosecution that I am not worried at all that perhaps I am going to disclose quite a few of my arguments to the Prosecution. I would prefer to have a readier Prosecution, not those who have this lack of readiness. For four years, they didn't read the material that I sent them. I am informing them about everything so they would be as ready as possible because this is a chance of a lifetime for me to prove my superiority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, this Chamber does not deal with superiority, Mr. Seselj, but with other determinations to be made. Mr. Seselj, you are aware that a pre-trial brief is limited to 15.000 words, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I demand, Mr. Orie, that you rule that my pre-trial brief can be of the same volume as the total pre-trial brief of the OTP, and it's about 75 pages, if my memory doesn't fail me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that request is on the record. We'll consider it. How long would you consider you would need to prepare your pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the day when you notify me, well, I think up until a month. That would be the maximum, because my people are already working on the brief. They have the main elements, now they have to put it all together nicely, and to compile it properly in line with the new reduced indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. May I address the Prosecution? The three weeks' time limit between the filing of the pre-trial brief and the Pre-Trial Conference is considered by this Chamber, but please comment on it if you take a different view. It's just a provisional position of the Chamber is mainly there in order to give an opportunity to the Prosecution to study it and to see whether it would like to deal with it in the opening statement. Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, does the Prosecution, first of all, take a similar position? And second, if there would be less time between the Pre-Trial Conference and the filing of the pre-trial brief, would that bother you?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have studied the Rules and of course 65 ter(F) is mandatory and there is these three weeks' period in there, but we think according to Rule 54, the Trial Chamber is in a position to override this time limit. This is actually the position that we take. But from the purpose of the Rule 65 ter(F), which is actually to enable everyone involved, including the Judges, to be aware of the Defence, we think the time limit that is necessary to comply with is that the pre-trial brief, the Defence pre-trial brief should be available to everyone and the Judges before the trial starts. We do not think it's necessarily to have to be three weeks, but before the -- before the Pre-Trial Conference, but it needs to be available at least at the moment when the taking of the evidence starts so that the Judges and the Prosecution is fully aware what the Defence is and can actually ask the appropriate questions to the witnesses that come up. I have actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you one question to start with. You're referring to Rule 54, not to 127. Is there any specific reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour. Because 127 refers to -- it says here "Save as provided by paragraph (C), a Trial Chamber or Pre-Trial Judge may, on good cause being shown by motion." We saw that Rule 127 actually needs an action from one of the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And therefore we thought Rule 54 would actually be more appropriate when the action is actually coming from the Bench itself. That's why I refer not to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's clear why you have chosen to refer to Rule 54. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I actually want to make a proposal because I think that nobody in this courtroom, in particular not the accused, would actually want to delay the trial. Everybody wants to actually start the trial. And I was thinking how to facilitate both, that is having a pre-trial brief in front of everyone before the evidence starts, and having not a -- one-month delay of trial. And I actually -- and my colleagues agree to this. We felt it would be probably a solution that to -- to set a deadline for filing of a pre-trial brief in relation to Hrtkovci only because -- in most likely in this year, we will only hear evidence on Hrtkovci. And if the accused will actually prepare a pre-trial brief on Hrtkovci only, giving a page limit of perhaps 10, 15 pages, and that -- if that would be available before the trial starts, let's say in a deadline of ten days preparing this document in relation to Hrtkovci, and then taking into consideration the translation of the document that needs to be done, we could actually start by the end of this month with the trial. The remainder of the pre-trial brief related to all other issues that are here in the indictment and at stake could be filed during the Christmas break, in January. That's actually a rather practical proposal. Perhaps the situation could be solved without delaying the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you heard the submissions made by Madam Uertz-Retzlaff -- let me just finish, please. The submissions one -- I would say, fundamentally, taking the position that a pre-trial brief should be file before the start of the trial. I have not asked yet, but we'll perhaps do that in the second trial, whether that would be the same as well if the opening statement is delayed until the beginning of the defence case. She further suggested that you would not want to delay the start of the trial. She pointed at the fact that the evidence to be heard in the very early stages of the trial would be limited to the events in Hrtkovci which we find mainly in, I think, paragraph 33 of the indictment. Would you please give your views on these practical, procedural, and also to some extent, matters of principle, raised by Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are purely matters of principle, Mr. Orie. And I will strictly adhere to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. That is where I see my chance to be, to strictly abide by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the Rules say at least three weeks before the Pre-Trial Conference, not the beginning of the trial. All of a sudden, the Prosecution is in a hurry. I've been waiting for four years and I've been hurrying and now all of a sudden, they're in a hurry. Out of this material that was submitted to me by the Prosecution, I see that they still haven't translated into Serbian over 100.000 pages of documents that they handed over to Hooper, Van der Spoel and whoever. They say this for each and every document. This doesn't exist in the Serbian language. They still have to have this translated. For four years, they have been hoping that I would be denied the right to represent myself and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and the Appeals Chamber disappointed you, Mr. Seselj. Is that what you said -- you said that you would be hoping that you would be denied to represent yourself. Well, whatever the situation is, you are representing yourself at this moment. Mr. Seselj, you started to be a bit repetitious on complaints about disclosed material not translated to you that has been dealt with at an earlier stage. What kind of material should be disclosed to you, in what language, and what format. There is no need at this moment to repeat that. Is there anything else in response to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something new, Mr. Orie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I would appreciate if you would not interrupt me. Mr. Seselj, is there anything else in response to what Madam Uertz-Retzlaff addressed that you would like to bring to our attention?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are two things. First of all, I am going to submit a single pre-trial brief. Secondly, I am going to appeal. I am going to seek certification to appeal regarding your decision that the OTP can stick to their old text of the pre-trial brief. Thirdly, a very important matter. What I refer to is something that I got yesterday, so I am not repeating myself. I got this only yesterday and I found out that there is over 100.000 pages of documents that they just kept in the English language, they didn't have it translated into Serbian yet, hoping that I would not be able to represent myself. I'm not disappointed by the ruling of the Appeals Chamber but I claim that it is an illegal decision because it was made on the basis of a falsified appeal. They did not represent my wish. Whereas my right to defend myself is a natural inalienable right and I fight for it to the very end. It is not a right based on the ruling of the Appeals Chamber, it is a natural right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I misunderstood where you said "they would be hoping." I understood "I would be hoping." It surprised me a bit but it's now -- I have re-read it on the transcript and it's clear what you said and also that my -- what I said after that is irrelevant. Yes, Mr. Seselj, anything else you'd like to ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, I renew my request. Since last time, you refused me the explanation that my right to defend myself had been taken away, do you remember? I asked for three working days per week. I renew that, highlighting health concerns, because I had back surgery, I have asthma, I'm being treated for high blood pressure, and now I have ulcers in the upper part of my stomach, so that is a new reason. And there is another reason. I represent myself, so I need a bit more time during the course of one working week. So an optimum would be to have -- for me would be to have three working days per week as in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever the long-term scheduling will be, Mr. Seselj, you may be aware that although for other reasons a slower schedule has been granted at the request of Mr. Hooper, at that time, that this decision has not been reversed and that would go until Christmas. So therefore, until such a decision would be referred, we would sit, if the trial starts, as scheduled recently by the Trial Chamber which is a -- I think it was two days a week November, and three days a week, December. Second, you're talking about health concerns. It would certainly assist the Chamber that if there are any health concerns not being dealt with in the past yet, because I remember that we had some issues about your asthma, et cetera. If there's any new information, the Chamber would like to receive that, but preferably provided by qualified persons, that is, doctors or nurses who specifically deal with it. Then the last issue, you said you would seek a certificate to appeal the decision the Chamber rendered -- let me just see, it was the decision -- yes, that the Prosecution would not have to amend its pre-trial brief on the basis of the meanwhile reduced indictment. Do you apply for this orally and would you intend to give the reasons at this moment, or would you prefer to do that in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's much easier for me to do it orally, Mr. Orie. I believe that is a very important moment in these proceedings in line with the appropriate Rule in the Rules and that the speed of the trial and the fairness of the trial truly depends on that. That is what I can say off the top of my head. If you want me to do this in writing, I will do it even more thoroughly. So I am invoking the appropriate Rule in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I am convinced that all the necessary requirements have been met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the Chamber will consider whether your preference to apply orally to such a certificate is the appropriate procedure to be followed and we'll come back to that after the break. Yes, I'm looking at the clock, and since the Chamber has a few matters to consider at this moment, we'd like to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will resume in half an hour. Well, let's say a little bit more, quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will resume the hearing. The Chamber has considered some of the issues that were raised before the break. First, Mr. Seselj, the Chamber would like to pay a bit more attention to the special defences. The Chamber, on the basis of what we heard from you, is not yet fully convinced that you make a clear distinction between unique defences and special defences under Rule 67. Also, the Chamber brings to your attention that the duty to notify the Prosecution exists if there is a special defence, and that only such notification of a truly special defence under Rule 67 would trigger an obligation for the Prosecution to respond to that under Rule 67(A)(ii). The Chamber invites you at this moment and -- to better inform us about what your special defences are, just in one or two short lines. For example, I give you two examples, one on the basis of the Rules. If, for example, if you would want to raise a defence of alibi, then you could briefly set that out by saying: My defence will be that I was not at place X at time Y as charged in the indictment in paragraph 32. That would clearly identify a special defence. And just to give another example and referring to what you said earlier, you said, and I tried to do it also in two lines, to show you how you could inform the Chamber about your special defences, you would have identified what you said before as to hate speech in the following way: My special defence is that other political leaders both from the former Yugoslavia and from Europe, United States, wherever you want to refer to, used worse language than I ever did when they delivered their speeches. That's just two lines of an indication of what then the special defence would be. The Chamber is inviting you to do so because, on the basis of what you have submitted until now, the Chamber is not yet convinced that defences you refer to constitute special defences and Rule 67(A). Therefore, you are invited now to give us in such a short way what exactly you define as being your special defences. You may do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to explain that although it's difficult to do in such a short period of time. In terms of the translation or interpretation of your words, the interpreter made a distinction between a unique and special defence. Did you actually say that? Was that was said in the source language? I believe that a distinction can be made between a regular and special defence. A regular defence is a defence that is applied in all the cases that you had until now before the International Tribunal. The Prosecutor bears the burden of proof and the accused defends himself that he is not guilty or not as guilty as the Prosecutor insists. Now what I'm doing here is applying a special defence, namely, something that is quite different from everything else you've had before this Tribunal so far. Through it, I'm trying to prove that historical circumstances, in which I operated, do not allow the Prosecution at all to base their indictment on what they are basing it. That is the core of my special defence, if you understood me better now. So historical circumstances. From that context, the Prosecution takes random statements of mine or fabricated statements of mine. They even did that, and then they based the indictment on that. That is an untenable method. That is why, as I investigated through my legal advisors and professional team, these special historical circumstances, I prove that the indictment is a total failure. It's amiss. That is as far as hate speech is concerned. As for portraying the causes of war and its consequences, that is where the Vatican and the Roman Popes played the major role. It's not something that accidentally took place in the Balkans between 1991 and 1993. That is the period of my indictment or up to 1995, or say 1999, that other indictments include. But it is very clearly placed in a certain historical context spanning a 1.000 years. That is what makes my defence special and something -- and it is something that you did not have before this Tribunal so far. That is the way I act in the case of some presumed witnesses. I don't know whether these persons will actually testify in my trial but they already have a subscription, so to speak, to testify in different trials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I invited you to identify one or more special defences under Rule 67(A). You are now dwelling on issues as whether witnesses will come up. That's not specifically what I asked you. Are there any other -- you refer to the historical context in general terms. You also specifically refer to the Roman -- the Vatican and Roman Popes. Is there any other special defence you would like to identify so that we are better able to understand whether the Prosecution would be under any obligation to respond.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, I'll do my best to explain it to you, that this concept of mine, of a special defence, is a unique one. It consists of several elaborates and several topics. One of the topics is the role of the Pope and of the Vatican within the unique concept of a special defence. Second topic is an analysis of hate speech in the western press, in the western public, by western politicians, by Muslim politicians in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croat politicians in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is to say that all of this is within a unique concept of a special defence of refuting the portrayal of general historical circumstances that the Prosecution has resorted to in my case and in all cases before that starting with Dusko Tadic. I am challenging their approach to the history of the Balkans from 1991 until 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you said one topic was the context, the second one was the hate speech in the western press. Is there a third topic you would specifically want to draw attention to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third topic is joint criminal enterprise. The fourth topic are my public speeches about the war and telling volunteers and Serbs in general that they have to abide by international laws of war, that they have to fight in a chivalrous manner on the front line, how they should treat prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, is that topic that you challenge that this could be proven; is that what your defence would be?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, I really don't know how we cannot be on the same wavelength here. I am trying to challenge the indictment through a concept of a special defence and I'm challenging the indictment in a way that was never done by anyone before this Tribunal. I am challenging the approach of the Prosecution to the problem through my special defence. As for my regular defence, to do that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, it's just not clear. You say the fourth topic are my public speeches. There are a few opportunities. You say I want to address this public speeches in their historical context and that's my special defence. Or you say, I want to challenge that I ever gave such speeches and that's my special defence, or whatever. But I'd like you to explain to me in one or two lines what, exactly, in relation to your public speeches, your special defence would be?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first study, the first segment which I submitted to the OTP concerned excerpts from my public speeches. This was about 300 pages. With that study, I submit I -- here to the OTP, here in the courtroom, 80 of my published books which contained the former -- the point is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to interrupt you. I did not invite you to say how many pages you submitted to the Prosecution. I invited you to identify what your special defence in relation to, as you said, your fourth topic, public speech, was. I gave you a few of the possible examples. I invite you now to explain not the whole of the special defence, but to identify what your special defence is. You challenge that it happened or you say I want to put that in historical context or you want to say it happened, but others did it. Everything is fine, but please tell us what your special defence is in relation to your public speech.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards my public speeches, my special defence is that in the context of those speeches, which I portray in integral form, everything which the OTP ascribes to me on the basis of those witnesses is untenable because my public speeches testify to one thing, several false witnesses of the Prosecution say something else. My regular defence will be to challenge these statements of those witnesses once they appear here. My special defence is to contest the possibility for such statements of mine to have been made at all, the statements that are ascribed to me by false witnesses. I hope that I was clear now. So from what I have submitted, it's quite obvious that what the false witnesses are saying is impossible. Once I submit my regular defence, I will adduce argumentation to prove that the false witnesses are wrong, the argumentation which I have at my disposal. My special concept demonstrates that what is in the indictment and in the fabricated witnesses statements is completely untenable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has listened to you, Mr. Seselj. What you have told us until now is that a comprehensive statement of what your special defence will be.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That cannot be an exhaustive description. This is a very simplified description in order for you to understand me much more easily, Mr. Orie. It is too complex for me to be able to put it in a nutshell. What I'm trying to do is to illustrate the point of special defence for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll consider that, Mr. Seselj. Yes. Another matter which the Chamber would like to deal with is the certificate you applied for, the certificate to appeal the decision of this Trial Chamber not to order the Prosecution to amend its pre-trial brief. You have given us the reasons. As you certainly are aware of, the application of the -- of Rule 73, the test to -- the test for obtaining a certificate being that the decision involves a issue that would significantly affect a fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial, and for which, in the opinion of the Trial Chamber, an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber may materially advanced the proceedings. That test is of a highly legal technical nature, although you've given already reasons for your oral application for a certificate. The Chamber wanted to stress again the technical character of this test. I would like to give you an opportunity to reconsider whether the reasons you had given already would need any -- whether anything should be added to that or whether you are satisfied with the reasons, or that you would say: Give me an opportunity after the next break so that I can better inform you whether I gave the complete reasons for my application or not. We'll leave that to you, but the Chamber wanted to draw your attention to this technical character of the test to be applied which, of course, would require a similar technical approach in the application to be made. I don't know whether you want -- would like to respond to it right away and say, no, what I've said is sufficient or you would say, no, give me until after the next break and then I'll give you an answer. It's up to you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should be very brief, Mr. Orie. My view, the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution is, in terms of importance, the second-most important legal act of the Prosecution in the pre-trial stage. It is upon the content of the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution that the very good measure, not as important as the indictment, but in a very good measure, depends my concept of defence, my own pre-trial brief, my accused's statement, and my conduct of the questioning of the Prosecution witnesses. So that I have to bear in mind not only the indictment but also the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution in that entire process. If the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution remains as it was, I can face a dilemma to have to appraise something which does not exist in the indictment but does exist in the OTP's pre-trial brief in terms whether I should pay sufficient attention or not or any attention, and the expeditiousness of the trial depends on that. So my own pre-trial brief shall be much more precise if it is based on a single and revised text of the OTP's pre-trial brief. After all, Mr. Orie, the minute the modified amended indictment was confirmed, the OTP immediately had to produce a new pre-trial brief in accordance with the Rules, rather than submit an addition to its original or old pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anything else you would like to raise under Rule 73 as far as the reasons for the request for certification are concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I should like to voice my conviction that it is upon the affirmative resolution of my appeal that the fair and expeditious conduct of the trial depends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you consider this to be then the complete reasons or would you like to have an opportunity later today to add anything to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, these are general reasons in principle. If I were to address you in written form, I would go into more detail, but right now, I'm trying to exercise -- to express myself as concisely as possible and I believe that I have been quite clear. If you consider it necessary for me to state these things in writing, I can do so but I believe that it would be better for us to stick to the oral procedure because in that case, you can bring a decision faster, which decision, I believe, will be the same whether I state my request orally or in writing. But if there are any quandaries in respect of my request, I am prepared to make a written submission within an appropriate period, namely, within seven days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber does not insist on you making this request or giving the reasons in writing, and follows your suggestion to deal with the matter orally, and informs you that if you would like to add anything, you have an opportunity to do so today during this hearing. Another matter, Mr. Seselj, you raised was about the audio equipment. I told you that you would have an opportunity to further explain to us what was on your mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is a very important question and that you will have the patience to hear me out, Mr. Orie. The Prosecution, yesterday, informed, and I haven't quite added this up, but this is over 100.000 pages of documents. This was submitted this summer. This is 66 ter, 65(A) evidential material to Hooper, Van der Spoel et cetera. So over 100.000 pages in all. Now, I feel, since now the audio tapes and the audio player have become current, that the OTP is actually not prepared to translate all this into the Serbian language for me so that they are going to shower me with audio material. I don't know what that concerns. It's probably hearing of witnesses in other cases, statements of witnesses, what have you, et cetera. Of course you can decide that that be submitted to me in audio form, but 100.000 pages of audio material is at least 200.000 minutes because, of course, you know how the examination of witnesses goes with the simultaneous interpretation and so on and so forth. So you want me to listen in my prison cell to 200.000 minutes of material, that equals to 6.000 hours -- no, 3.000 hours, rather. 3.000 hours. Now you can calculate how many days that would be, about 400 days. Now you find me a psychiatrist who will tell you if I listen to that for eight hours a day, if we presume that, can one remain in his right mind if one listens to audio cassettes for eight hours a day for 400 days. That is absolutely impossible. That's one thing. Then another thing, we have over 2.000.000 pages of documents which they tried to serve on me in electronic form. Now they have to give it to me in hard copy, on paper. It goes without saying that will not take 400 days. If they try hard enough, it can be resolved within 10 or 15 days. Then again, there is another problem. If I receive all that material on paper, you know, it is property of intelligent people to be able to distinguish between the material from the immaterial, so I will try to be intelligent. I will leaf through that material and try to separate what I believe is of consequence. So I'm leafing through these papers and I come across things, I note things down and I prepare myself. That is, if I receive 100.000 pages of paper. If, however, I receive 100.000 pages on audio cassettes, then I cannot proceed in this way to make the proper selection. I have to listen to it all. How? How? Explain it to me. Of course I can do it for 25 hours a day if I get up an hour earlier, but can one preserve one's mental health in that way? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the whole issue started with the progress report made by the registrar on the availability of equipment that would allow you to listen to audio recordings. I now do understand, and that's perhaps a related issue, although not exactly the same, that you are strongly opposed against receiving or having disclosed to you any material in audio because it would be an impossible task for you to listen to it all. That is a bit beside the facilities given to you, but at least it's now on the record what objections you are raising in respect of this in general terms, referring to numbers of pages that were, as you said, recently disclosed. Any other matter in relation to the audio?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, a priori, I do not object to being given some material in audio form as well but it should be something which I can manage physically speaking. I'm not categorically against. I can receive it all in audio and video form, but to the extent that I can manage and handle it up to a maximum of 8 hours a day because one cannot concentrate more than that. If it is on paper, I can proceed much more quickly, I can work much more quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear that you prefer to receive the material on paper. You do not categorically say I would not receive material in audio format but you are especially complaining about the bulk of the material which would be too much to digest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, is there anything you'd like to add or to submit in respect of this? And I'm not seeking new debate on the form of disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one point. You have received from the Prosecution the tables that we provided. Mr. Seselj has them also in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that about witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's about the total number of pages of transcript and associated exhibits. That is one table where we list actually the witnesses and their materials, and also we have provided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has that been made available to Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, in the Serbian language and at a time also, our disclosure log that we also provided in both languages. And as you -- I just refer you to these two documents and I -- when I look at them, I cannot arrive at the number of pages that actually the accused just mentioned. I just refer you to the table and see for yourself. It's -- I can't get -- I don't understand how he gets these numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will carefully look at the size of the material disclosed either recently or in the past and what it would take to prepare for the examination of witnesses. In the beginning, Prosecution witnesses, what it takes to prepare for the cross-examination of witnesses. Of course, it should all be looked at in its context but thank you for referring us to the information you have provided in this respect. Then Mr. Seselj, are there any other matters you'd like to have put on the agenda for today? Because what the Chamber has in mind is to take a little bit more time to deliberate on the issue of pre-trial briefs, if possible, reach a decision and pronounce that decision today after a bit of a longer break than usual, then dependent on whether we can reach a decision or not, also to possibly deliver decisions on protective measures. And then at the end, of course, we would like to know whether there are any other matters that we should discuss during this Status Conference. What I would like to know is whether there are any such other matters you would like to raise or Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, you would like to raise. So if you would like to add anything to what I just mentioned as being on the agenda today.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to agenda items, I would actually like your opinion on our filings 89(F), 92 ter because we have made these substantial filings quite sometime in advance but of course we are aware that in other Trial Chambers, such filings are either done immediately before a witness testifies or actually orally only and we would like to hear guidelines from the Trial Chamber how they would like to proceed in this regard. That's the one point. And the other one is actually a question of whether you would like us to address the certification issue because Mr. Saxon is actually in a position to do that orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course -- well, if I may take it that Mr. Seselj has preferred to deal with it orally and that he has, by now, given the reasons he wanted to give. Mr. Saxon, you have an opportunity to respond to that. At the same time, if Mr. Seselj later today, would like to add something to the reasons, then of course you would have an opportunity to respond to that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly, I'd like to correct one comment made a few moments ago by the accused. The accused suggested that after the Prosecution filed its modified amended indictment, it had to produce immediately a new pre-trial brief. That is incorrect. What the Prosecution produced was an addendum to its original pre-trial brief and that was only because there were allegations that had been added to the indictment in the modified amended indictment and so there were allegations added and only those allegations that were added were addressed in the addendum to the pre-trial brief. This situation is very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Mr. Saxon, you are now going to the substance of the matter rather than to the criteria for a certificate, isn't it? I have read the criteria for the certificate and -- unless you say it has a direct impact on those criteria, but then please explain to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, in the Prosecution's submission, Your Honour, the accused has not met the criteria for certification under Rule 73(B). He has not established how the Chamber's decision would affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial, and how an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber would advance these proceedings. Rule 73 bis (D), which was the basis of the decision by the Trial Chamber, says nothing regarding the -- a submission of additional brief and that is because this Rule applies to the scope and quantity of the evidence, not the quantity of the evidence or the allegations. Therefore, Your Honour, fairness in this case does not require additional explanation in the form of an additional pre-trial brief. That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Then any other matter you would like to raise, apart from the 92 ter and now the response to the certificate request? Anything other ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. Mr. Seselj, is there anything you would like to have added to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, I should like to add something that I haven't said before. According to the directive on the length of briefs, you caution me that the pre-trial brief could have 15.000 words. The OTP's -- the first pre-trial brief had around 15.000 words or so, don't take my word for it, I can't be quite sure or precise, but the additional OTP's brief was about 7.500 words, counting the pages, and they never asked for your leave to allow them to exceed that number. And now they don't want to integrate that text. I want them to integrate it to reduce it to 50 pages.
