Or if you should allow them to increase the number of pages, I should like to be given a like permission to increase my number of pages. And another thing which I should like to draw your attention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I just notice at this moment that the request to have a total number of pages the same as the Prosecution used both in its pre-trial brief and the supplement to it is already on the record, so there was no need to repeat that. Then the second issue, whether they have to reduce it to 50 pages, the Chamber ruled that there was no need at this moment to file a new pre-trial brief. So that matter has been dealt with and your request for a certificate is pending. Please, any other matter for the agenda?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Orie, I do have something, but if you will allow me, I should like to go back to what Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff has stated. She tried to deny my statement that we are talking about 200.000 pages or so. But take a look at this document, item 10 of this document disclosed by Vojislav Seselj. You will see that it indicates 207.000 pages, that is just one document, just one dispatch from the OTP to me. I was actually very conservative when I said I refused to accept -- to receive 200.000 pages in electronic form, not including those that were -- that were actually submitted to Mr. Van der Spoel. So you can see that this is 207.210 pages. So it seems that I am better acquainted with the documents that the OTP submitted to me yesterday than Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. I'm really amazed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think perhaps some distinction should be made between disclosure under Rule 66 and disclosure under Rule 68, but it seems that that might explain the difference of view, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was actually concentrating on the material that was in English because that's what Mr. Seselj had referred to. And I was actually under the impression he was referring to transcripts and the like, but what he is now mentioning is B/C/S material that was provided on DVDs related to Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's on the record, your position, and Mr. Seselj, your response is now on the record as well. Is there any other matter you'd like to add to the agenda?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I address another question, Mr. Orie? Please look at items 24 and 26. This was disclosed under 65(A) and 65 ter. Item 24, 12.150 pages of transcript in the English language or 232 audio tapes in the Serbian, which I should be given to listen to. Item 26, 40.000 pages in English. So we are not talking only about 68 -- Rule 68 materials, but we are talking about all the Rules on the basis of which the OTP submits material to me. So far, on paper, and in the Serbian, this is all that I have received from the survey made by the OTP and I never refused it, except in one case, when they just submitted a batch of documents without even a title as to what it contained. So that one I refused. I sent them a letter asking them to indicate precisely what was in the batch and to put the documents in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, any need to respond to the last remarks by Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this reference to receipt number 24, that's correct, that's actually what I was referring to. That's the English transcript and the audio files in Serbian language. In relation to receipt number 26, just this point, the 40 pages of English are actually the translation of the 34 pages in B/C/S. English is usually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says 40.000. Is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, 40.000 pages of English and 34.000 pages of B/C/S. That's actually the translation -- referring to the original and the translation. It's not that you have to add those to come up with something like 70.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's still 34.000 pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the Chamber will -- Mr. Seselj, the Chamber will certainly not ignore the issue of what it takes to prepare for the cross-examination of witnesses during the presentation of the Prosecution's case and what material will be used, and what it takes to prepare for cross-examination. And the Chamber will not -- will also include in its considerations the number of pages and the amount of the material that is relevant for those witnesses and for their testimony. Any other issue, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Orie. You see, these 40.000 pages in English or 34.000 pages in Serbian, the Prosecutor never tried to serve that on me. It was only given to Hooper, never to me. As for item 24, they tried to serve on me 232 audio recordings on computer disks and that is why I refused it. And you should do the math. For 12 and a half thousand pages, even if they did have audio tapes, how much time would be necessary to hear all of that? Then another thing that's also important. The Trial Chamber receives all documents on paper, in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, before we continue, you said you refused to receive that because it was in electronic format. If you would persist in that, then the whole issue seems to not be very relevant. I mean what you say: I've got no time to listen to the material which I refuse to accept.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that you are willing to accept audio files and -- because on the table, it reads that you refused and returned it. If that's not correct, please tell us. If it is correct ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you everything, Mr. Orie. We really have to clarify this. Electronic recordings are one thing and audio recordings are a different thing. I am refusing to receive anything in electronic format, but I did not refuse audio recordings if these are cassettes that are used on a cassette player. I am refusing everything that has to do with computers because I refuse to use a computer and I am fully clear on that. I want to receive audio recordings but you should assess how much a normal person can take and how much time it takes to hear all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, audio means you can listen to it. Video means you can listen to it and you can view it, whether it's on a tape or whether it's on a DVD or on a CD. I then think I perfectly understood that you are not willing to accept audio material if it is provided to you in such a way that you should put a disc in a computer or any player that could reproduce that and then listen to it. Is that correct? And you insist on receiving those audio in, I would say, the classical tape format. Is that a correct understanding; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only agree to classical format because everything that has to do with a computer is something that I categorically refuse and I stick to that. I am not going to receive anything that's related to computers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that you are not behaving -- or at least that the acceptable format of disclosure in the 4th of July decision of this Chamber is not accepted by you and that you will not seek to access any material that is disclosed to you in any other format than the classical audio or the classical video, that is, tape format. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were very precise. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Any other matter for the agenda, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have one more brief question. I have problems with studying the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and this problem is caused by the Registry. I asked the Registry several times to familiarise me with the jurisprudence and I requested different kinds of documents from the jurisprudence. So far, the Registry submitted to me only decisions, first and second instance, and very rarely some other decisions in addition to judgements. However, when I asked for the Limaj, Bala, Musliu judgement, the Registry told me that existed only in the English or Albanian languages. Before that, I asked for judgements of the Rwanda Tribunal, first and second instance, I was refused on that too, so I had to pay myself for translations from English of some judgements that I was interested in. But now since I'm asking about judgements of this Tribunal only, I ask from you that you instruct the Registry to provide me with copies. Limaj, Bala, Musliu case is one of the more important cases before this Tribunal and I really want to familiarise myself with that judgement of first instance in its Serbian translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I remember, this is a new episode in a matter that has been decided upon before, but we'll consider the matter. Your request is on the record. Any other matter to be raised for the agenda, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Orie, this is not a new episode, because so far, I have received practically all judgements of this Tribunal. Perhaps I haven't got a few of the latest ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I did not invite you to further expound on the matter, but I asked you whether there was any other matter you would like to raise for the agenda.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Then we will adjourn and the Chamber might need a bit more time to see whether it can reach decisions mainly on the pre-trial brief matter. That could easily take us another 40 to 60 minutes and then we'll have a short last session in which we'll deliver decisions to the extent that we have reached such decisions. I -- therefore everyone is asked to remain on standby, at least on from five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the Chamber will deliver a few decisions. Mr. Seselj, the Chamber has decided to allow you to file a pre-trial brief by the 23rd of November, 2006. The word limit you are granted is 38.500 typed words, which is just above the total number of words used by the Prosecution for its pre-trial brief and the supplement to that brief. Your pre-trial brief should deal with the Hrtkovci allegations, if you have any submissions to make in relation to these allegations. It should also deal with the main aspects of the Defence case, and as many other specific matters as you are able to manage within the time frame. You will be entitled to supplement your pre-trial brief by a submission to be filed by Monday, the 8th of January, 2007. The supplement, if any, should not repeat any material that you will include in your pre-trial brief. The supplement should not have the effect of extending the total word limit. This means that if you would use 30.000 words for your pre-trial brief, you will have a maximum of only 8.500 words left for any supplement. A written decision giving the full reasons will follow in due course. There will be another Status Conference on the 22nd of November, 2006, and we are scheduled on the 22nd of November in the morning hours, so that would be at 9.00 in the morning. The Pre-Trial Conference will be held on the 27th of November, 2006, to be followed immediately by the start of the trial and therefore the opening statement of the Prosecution. The Prosecution should not take more than two and a half hours for its opening statement. Mr. Seselj, you will have the same amount of time to make your delayed opening statement pursuant to Rule 84 at the beginning of the Defence case, if it ever comes to that. Mr. Seselj, you will be allowed to make an unsworn statement under Rule 84 bis on the 28th of November, 2006. We are then sitting in the morning hours. The Chamber will allow you two hours for this statement to be given under the control of the Chamber as provided for by Rule 84 bis. The hearing of Prosecution witnesses will commence on the 6th of December, 2006. There will then be six consecutive days following that date to hear Prosecution witnesses before the winter recess. This, as far as pre-trial briefs and scheduling is concerned. There are a few more matters, some of them relating to witness protection, I'd like to deal with. Mr. Seselj, at the last Status Conference, you said, and I quote: "A few moments ago, when we referred to the question of sending out confidential material, your decisions contained that question, too, and you were blaming me for things like that and that is why you were imposing counsel on me. "The case that you referred to from last year was the case when I telephoned a friend of mine, a party member, who is an official of the city government in Novi Sad, and told him the name of a person who is a criminal and a war profiteer. And I heard through the grapevine that he should appear as a protected witness in some of the trials in The Hague. I had no idea that he was meant to be a witness in my own trial, too." That's the end of the quote. Mr. Registrar, I'd like to go into closed session for a short period of time, which will mean that the public gallery should be empty as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber has been informed that the Prosecution is able to commence the presentation of its case with the witnesses for Hrtkovci as well as with witness VS-017. This is a total of 10 witnesses, although we understand that the witnesses VS-1137 and VS-1138 may not be called, due to illness or other reasons. We have received motions for protective measures in relation to three of these witnesses. VS-017 was assigned a pseudonym for these proceedings by a decision dated the 16th of December, 2004. In the Prosecutor's eighth motion for protective measures, dated the 7th of July, 2006, the Prosecution additionally requested delayed disclosure of the witness's identity and unredacted statements until 30 days before the scheduled date of the witness's testimony. The latter request, if you would call that witness in December, is now moot. It's approximately 30 days, and the Chamber hereby orders the Prosecution to immediately disclose to the accused, in unredacted format, the material related to witness VS-017. In its eighth motion, the Prosecution also requested that VS-017 be granted face and voice distortion during testimony. The eighth motion was received in translation by the accused on the 27th of July, 2006. A reply from the accused has not been received by the Chamber. According to information provided by the Prosecution, VS-017 and his family live in an area where the risk of retaliation for cooperation with the Tribunal is very high. VS-017 is expected to give evidence of the involvement of the accused and a number of his alleged associates in crimes. VS-017 is very fearful that he or his family will be harmed if it becomes known that he appeared as a witness before the Tribunal. These circumstances justify the grounds of face and voice distortion during testimony, as requested by the Prosecution. I am requesting the indulgence of the interpreters and the technicians. I have another approximately two and a half page to be read and remaining issues we'll deal with at the Status Conference next week, but these are decisions which are important to be delivered. I see nodding yes. Thank you for your understanding. VS-053 was assigned a pseudonym for these proceedings by a decision dated the 27th of May, 2005. In the Prosecutor's eighth motion for protective measures, the Prosecution additionally requested face and voice distortion during testimony. As the Chamber mentioned before, a reply from the accused to the eighth motion has not been received by the Chamber. According to information provided by the Prosecution, VS-053 is expected to testify about crimes committed by an alleged associate of the accused. VS-053 and his family live in an area where the risk of retaliation for cooperation with this Tribunal is high. These circumstances justify the grant of face and voice distortion during testimony. VS-054 was assigned a pseudonym for these proceedings by a decision dated the 6th of July, 2005. The same decision granted delayed disclosure of the witness's identifying information until 30 days prior to the commencement of trial. In the Prosecutor's eighth motion for protective measures, the Prosecution requested that the delayed disclosure take place not later than 30 days prior to the commencement of trial, but -- no, I did -- I misread. The Prosecution requested that the delayed disclosure take place not 30 days prior to the commencement of trial, but rather, 30 days prior to the scheduled date of the witness's testimony. The latter request now is moot as well, if this witness will be called in the month of December during the first six days. And the Chamber therefore hereby orders the Prosecution to immediately disclose to the accused, in unredacted format, the material related to Witness VS-054. In its eighth motion, the Prosecution also requested that VS-054 be granted face and voice distortion during testimony. According to information provided by the Prosecution, VS-054 frequently travels for work-related reasons to an area where the risk of retaliation for cooperation with the Tribunal is high. VS-054 is expected to testify about crimes committed by an alleged associate of the accused who continues to live in the area. The witness has raised concerns for his personal security and is fearful that his public testimony at the Tribunal will jeopardise his safety when travelling to the relevant area. These circumstances justify the grant of face and voice distortion during testimony. The three witnesses with protective measures should be scheduled by the Prosecution to appear in December. In the interests of the smooth commencement of the trial, the Chamber has decided ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the interests of the smooth commencement of the trial, the Chamber has decided to order the Prosecution to immediately provide the accused with the material relating to the Hrtkovci witnesses whom the Prosecution intends to call, as well as with the material relating to VS-017. The Chamber exceptionally invites the Prosecution to consider providing this material to the accused in hard copy and in a language the accused understands. The Chamber wishes to emphasise, that in accordance with our decision on the form of disclosure, dated the 4th of July, the Prosecution is not obliged to provide any material to the accused in hard copy. The decision does require that the accused be provided with equipment and technical support to make effective use of material disclosed to him in electronic format. In the future, if the accused does not avail himself of this equipment and technical support which is offered to him, he will be choosing to deprive himself of access to disclosed material. In the present instance, however, in order to prevent any further delays to the start of the trial, we exceptionally invite the Prosecution to accept this burden, to the benefit of the accused. The Prosecution is required to arrange for the testimony of the accused in the Milosevic case to be provided to the accused in audio format. This is material which might be used in the examination of one of these witnesses to be called in December. The testimony of the expert witness Ewa Tabeau, also from the Milosevic case, must also be provided to the accused in audio format. The Registry is requested to ensure that the accused is provided with reasonable assistance for the purpose of effectively utilising material disclosed in audio format. As to the admission into evidence of the material relating to the aforementioned witnesses, decisions on this matter will be deferred to the time when the witnesses appear to testify. The Chamber is aware that the Prosecution has filed a motion, dated the 13th of October, 2006, for Witness VS-053 to testify through videolink, due to health reasons. As far as the Chamber knows, this motion has not yet been translated or served upon the accused. The Chamber kindly requests the Registry to inform the legal staff of this Chamber as soon as the document has been translated and served upon the accused. Finally, the Chamber informs the parties, that in cases where a rapid decision is required of the Chamber, and where it is appropriate, it may be more efficient to make motions orally before the Chamber, having requested permission to do so. These were the decisions the Chamber wanted to deliver. There are no other matters at this moment on the agenda the Chamber would like to deal with. Where I earlier said the Status Conference of next week, of course, I wanted to refer to the Status Conference scheduled for the 22nd of November, 2006, which is, of course, two weeks from now and not next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There being no further items on the agenda, and announcing that if Mr. Seselj -- I was just saying that I would announce that if there is any further matter that should be discussed, it should be done at the next Status Conference. Of course, I wouldn't -- I do not know what you intended to say, but if you -- you have 30 seconds to explain to me what you wanted to raise, not to raise it as such, because then the Chamber will decide whether it's really urgent enough to ask for the further indulgence of the interpreters and the technicians or whether we could deal with the matter on the next Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to do it in 20 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you're invited to use the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just now trampled on your earlier decisions to have all the protected witnesses named disclosed to me a month before the trial. So none -- in none of the cases, it will be a month. Second, you are cautioning me of something which happened prior to the appellate decision, which actually -- since the decision waiving my right to representation. You have already experienced a fiasco with your decision with the decision of the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you've used your 20 seconds. Nothing you said in these 20 seconds causes me to not delay any further matter to the next Status Conference. We stand adjourned.
